claim: The Yarlung Tsangpo / Medog hydropower project has a planned installed capacity of about 60 GW and expected annual generation of about 300 TWh.
bestEstimate: Installed capacity: ~60 GW (60,000 MW) as the most-cited planned figure, though credible estimates range up to ~70-81 GW depending on how many of the cascade stations and how much of the ~70 GW technically-exploitable Great Bend potential is captured. Expected annual generation: ~300 TWh/year (300 billion kWh), i.e. roughly 3x the Three Gorges Dam (~22.5 GW / ~95-112 TWh).
reasoning: The claim's two headline numbers are consistently reported across independent sources (Wikipedia, Power Magazine, CNN, The Diplomat, Jamestown, and Chinese-language outlets including Guancha and Xinhua-derived reporting). The project (officially the Motuo/Medog Hydropower Station on the lower Yarlung Tsangpo / Brahmaputra) broke ground 19 July 2025, costs ~RMB 1.2 trillion (~USD 167-170 bn), uses a diversion-tunnel scheme through the Great Bend with five cascade stations, and targets ~2033 first operations. Two caveats prevent a stronger 'exact' framing: (1) China has NOT published a single official, definitive total capacity number — the project is described as secretive, so '~60 GW' is the most common figure but several reputable analyses cite 'more than 60 GW' or a 60-80 GW range (e.g., Jamestown: '60-80 GW' for the lower reaches; multiple sources: 'as high as 70 GW'; the basin's main-stream theoretical potential is ~80 GW and the Great Bend's technically exploitable potential ~70 GW). So '~60 GW' is best read as a conservative/lower-bound planned figure, not a hard cap. (2) The 300 TWh/year figure traces to Chinese reporting (China Energy News 2021; Ta Kung Pao 2025) and is the widely repeated 'triple Three Gorges' number; sources do not transparently reconcile it with the exact final capacity. Internal consistency check: 300 TWh / (60 GW x 8760 h) implies a ~57% capacity factor, which is physically reasonable for a high-head diversion hydro plant (at 70 GW it implies ~49%, also reasonable). Because the claim says 'about 60 GW' and 'about 300 TWh,' it accurately reflects the dominant planned figures; it is only mildly oversimplified in that capacity could ultimately be higher (up to ~70-81 GW) and no number is officially confirmed.

claim: The levelized cost of electricity (LCOE) from large hydropower is roughly $30-60/MWh (0.03-0.06 USD/kWh), and far-western Chinese hydro can be at the low end.
bestEstimate: Typical new large hydro LCOE ~$40-60/MWh (0.04-0.06 USD/kWh), with the global weighted average ~$57/MWh in 2023-2024; full project-level spread is much wider (~$20-190/MWh). Chinese large hydro averages ~$40/MWh (0.04 USD/kWh), among the lowest-cost regions globally, so the claim that far-western Chinese hydro sits at the low end is directionally correct.
reasoning: I independently re-derived this primarily from IRENA's Renewable Power Generation Costs reports (2023 and 2024 editions) and IRENA's Hydropower Costs database, cross-checked against Chinese on-grid tariff data. Key findings: (1) IRENA's global weighted-average LCOE for newly commissioned hydropower was 0.061 USD/kWh (2022), 0.057 USD/kWh (2023, $57/MWh), and ~0.057 USD/kWh (2024). This sits at the TOP of the claimed $30-60 band, so the claim's range is slightly optimistic as a description of the global average -- $30-60 better describes low-cost regions than the world average. (2) IRENA's regional decomposition for large hydro commissioned over the past decade: China and Brazil ~0.040 USD/kWh ($40/MWh); North America ~0.080 USD/kWh ($80/MWh); Europe ~0.120 USD/kWh ($120/MWh). This strongly confirms China is among the lowest-cost hydro regions, supporting the second half of the claim. (3) Project-level range is very wide -- IRENA's cost analysis cites roughly $0.02-0.19/kWh ($20-190/MWh) at a 10% cost of capital, so $30-60/MWh captures the central/typical band but not the full distribution; remote, high-civil-works, or storage-heavy projects (including some far-western Chinese mega-dams with long transmission) can exceed $60/MWh. (4) Cross-check: Chinese hydro on-grid benchmark tariffs run ~0.2-0.4 yuan/kWh (avg ~0.29 yuan/kWh, ~$0.04/kWh), consistent with the ~$40/MWh LCOE figure. Disagreements/nuances among sources: IRENA reports the China figure as a nationwide large-hydro average, NOT a far-western-specific number -- so the specific "far-western at the low end" framing is plausible and directionally right but not separately documented; far-western provinces (Tibet/Yunnan/Sichuan, e.g., Jinsha, Lancang, Yarlung Tsangpo basins) host China's cheapest sites due to high head and large unit sizes, but newer remote mega-projects can carry higher capital and transmission costs. The $30-60/MWh figure also assumes a moderate discount rate (~7-10%); at higher WACC, capital-intensive hydro LCOE rises substantially. Bottom line: the claim is supported as a typical-range statement, with the caveat that the global average is near the top of the range and the very low end (~$30/MWh) applies mainly to favorable, already-developed Chinese/Brazilian sites rather than new far-western mega-projects universally.

claim: UHVDC long-distance transmission loses on the order of ~1.5% per 1000 km (roughly 5-10% over 2000-3000 km) and adds on the order of $0.01-0.03/kWh in levelized transmission cost.
bestEstimate: Line losses: ~2.5-3.5% per 1000 km for typical ±800 kV UHVDC (1.5% per 1000 km is achievable ONLY at the world-leading ±1100 kV class, e.g. Changji-Guquan; general HVDC is ~3.5%/1000 km). PLUS a distance-independent converter-station loss of ~1.4-1.6% total (both ends combined, ~0.7-0.8% each). Realistic total over 2000-3000 km: roughly 6-10% (e.g. Xiangjiaba-Shanghai ±800 kV ~2000 km, ~7200 MW: under 7% total). Levelized transmission cost: ~$0.005-0.03/kWh, depending heavily on voltage, utilization and distance; ~$0.01-0.02/kWh is a fair central figure for well-utilized UHVDC, but a peer-reviewed 500 kV HVDC study reaches ~$0.026/kWh per 1000 km (~$0.04/kWh over 1000 miles).
reasoning:
I re-derived each component independently and found the claim directionally right but optimistic and conflated on the loss figure, while the cost figure is broadly defensible.

LOSS PER 1000 km: The 1.5%/1000 km number is real but cherry-picked: it is the headline efficiency of the world's first and highest-voltage line, the ±1100 kV Changji-Guquan project (3324 km, 12 GW), reported as 1.5%/1000 km and "less than 1/4 of a ±500 kV line." Treating this as representative of "UHVDC" generally is an overstatement. Independent benchmarks: Wikipedia and World Nuclear Association both cite ~3.5%/1000 km for general HVDC and 2.6% over 800 km (~3.25%/1000 km) for ±800 kV. Engineering sources put ±800 kV in a 2.5-4%/1000 km range (line only). So the typical ±800 kV UHVDC is ~2-2.5x the claimed 1.5%.

OMITTED CONVERTER LOSSES: The claim's per-km framing hides a critical, distance-independent term. AC/DC converter stations lose ~0.7-0.8% per end (National Grid), i.e. ~1.4-1.6% total round-trip regardless of length. This is why short links look bad on a %/1000-km basis and why the 1.5%/1000-km figure cannot simply be multiplied by distance.

TOTAL OVER 2000-3000 km: Here the claim's 5-10% band is reasonable and lands near reality, but for the right reasons only after adding converters. Xiangjiaba-Shanghai (±800 kV, ~2000 km, up to 7200 MW) is documented at under 7% total. Decomposing: ~2%/1000 km line at moderate load x2 = ~4% + ~1.5% converters ~ 5.5%, rising toward 7%+ at full load. The claim's stated 1.5%/1000 km would predict only ~3-4.5% line loss over 2000-3000 km, which would be too low without converters; the 5-10% total band quietly already absorbs the converter term the per-km figure ignored. So the two halves of the loss claim are internally inconsistent unless converter losses are folded into the second.

COST: $0.01-0.03/kWh is a defensible order-of-magnitude for levelized transmission cost. Real anchors: the peer-reviewed iScience paper (DeSantis et al. 2021) models 500 kV HVDC at ~$41.5/MWh per 1000 miles (~$0.026/kWh per 1000 km) - at/above the top of the band, and for a lower-voltage, lossy (12.9%/1000 mi) case. Clean Line Energy quoted ~$0.02/kWh all-in over 750 miles (developer claim, not peer-reviewed). Chinese ±800 kV projects (e.g. Gansu-Zhejiang, ~$4.8B, ~36 TWh/yr) imply much lower unit costs (sub-$0.01/kWh) because of very high utilization and amortization. So the band is correct but conflates per-1000-km cost with total cost: higher-voltage, well-loaded UHVDC sits at the low end (~$0.005-0.015/kWh), while lower-voltage or per-1000-km figures can exceed $0.03.

WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE: Loss per 1000 km ranges from 1.5% (±1100 kV best case) to 3.5% (general HVDC) to ~8%/1000 km equivalent (heavily-loaded 500 kV in the iScience study) - a 5x spread driven by voltage and loading. Cost spans roughly $0.005 to $0.04/kWh depending on voltage, utilization, distance and whether converter capex is included. Net: the claim is right in spirit (UHVDC is low-loss and adds 1-3 cents/kWh) but the 1.5%/1000 km loss figure is best-case not typical, and it omits the ~1.5% fixed converter-station loss.

claim: Datacenter-level energy per LLM output token is on the order of 0.3-4 Joules/token, i.e. roughly 1-10 million output tokens per kWh, depending on model size and batching.
bestEstimate: For mainstream, well-batched, non-reasoning inference on modern hardware (2024-2025), roughly 0.3-4 J/output token at the datacenter level is a defensible central range (~0.9-12 million output tokens/kWh). GPU-only optimized figures dip to ~0.15-0.4 J/token (>=9 million tokens/kWh). BUT the claimed range understates the high end: very large frontier models at high throughput reach ~40-120 J/token (~30k-90k tokens/kWh), and reasoning/test-time-scaling workloads multiply per-token energy 10-100x. A fairer all-in range is ~0.2 J/token (best case) to ~50-100+ J/token (frontier/reasoning, with overhead).
reasoning: I independently re-derived and cross-checked the numbers rather than trusting the claim. (1) Epoch AI (Josh You, 2025) estimates 0.3 Wh per ~500-token GPT-4o query at the cluster level (200B params/100B active MoE, H100 at 700W TDP x 70% power-util x ~1500W cluster-incl-overhead, 10% MFU). I recomputed: 0.3 Wh = 1080 J / 500 tokens = ~2.16 J/token = ~1.67 million tokens/kWh -- squarely inside the claimed range. (One auto-summary mis-stated this as 0.6 mJ/token; that is an arithmetic error -- the paper's own inputs give ~2 J/token.) (2) 'Where Do the Joules Go?' (arXiv 2601.22076) measures 0.15-0.31 J/token (Qwen3-32B) and ~0.4 J/token (Qwen3-235B FP8), GPU-only at large batch. (3) Lin 2025: 0.39 J/token (Llama3-70B FP8, 8xH100, batch 128, GPU-only). (4) Samsi 2023: ~3.5 J/token (LLaMA-65B, A100/V100) -- the historical upper bound of the claim. So the lower/middle of the claim is well supported. WHERE THE CLAIM IS OVERSIMPLIFIED / WRONG AT THE TOP END: TokenPowerBench (arXiv 2512.03024) reports 40-60 J/token for 405B-480B frontier models (Llama-3 405B, Falcon 180B, Qwen 480B) on 16xH100 under high-throughput load; Li 2023 reports ~120 J/token with realistic SLOs/overhead. Multiple sources (arXiv 2509.20241; Cell/Joule 2026) emphasize reasoning/test-time scaling multiplies per-token energy 10-100x; Epoch's own long-query estimate is 4.32 Wh (~13x baseline). SCOPE CAVEAT: the lowest figures (0.15-0.4 J/token) are GPU-only; AI accelerators are only ~50-70% of datacenter energy, and datacenter PUE adds ~10-30%, so full datacenter values are ~1.4-2x the GPU-only numbers -- which is exactly what pushes optimized cases up toward the claim's center. Net: the order-of-magnitude and the dependence on model size/batching are correct, and the range is right for typical optimized inference, but the 4 J/token ceiling is too low for frontier and reasoning workloads by 1-2 orders of magnitude.

claim: Global LLM token throughput in 2025 is on the order of 10^16 to 10^17 tokens per year and growing rapidly.
bestEstimate: Roughly 1.5 x 10^16 to 2 x 10^16 tokens/year as a late-2025 run-rate for major commercial LLM/API inference (input + output + reasoning + multimodal tokens). The true value sits near the BOTTOM of the claimed 10^16–10^17 band, not the middle. Earlier in 2025 it was lower (order 10^15/month aggregate, ~10^16/yr run-rate), so a full-year 2025 cumulative total is likely ~0.7–1.5 x 10^16 tokens, with the exit run-rate ~1.8–2.4 x 10^16/yr. Includes large measurement uncertainty (factor of ~2-3).
reasoning: I re-derived the figure bottom-up from disclosed provider numbers, all converted to a common basis. Google (the largest single discloser): 980 trillion tokens/month in July 2025 and 1.3 quadrillion (1.3x10^15)/month by Oct 2025 -> annualized 1.2-1.6x10^16/yr ALONE. Microsoft Azure/Foundry: ~50 trillion (5x10^13)/month -> ~6x10^14/yr. OpenAI: 6 billion tokens/min disclosed at Oct 2025 DevDay; I verified 6x10^9 x 60 x 24 x 30 = 2.6x10^14/month (~260T/mo, matching Beth Kindig's independent calc) -> ~3.1x10^15/yr. A multi-source aggregate (Fireworks AI citing Menlo Ventures' 2025 Mid-Year LLM Market Update plus OpenAI/Google announcements) puts the TOTAL LLM API market at ~1.5 quadrillion tokens/month = 50 trillion/day -> ~1.8x10^16/yr. These independent lines converge on ~1.5-2x10^16 tokens/yr as a late-2025 run-rate. That lands inside the claimed 10^16-10^17 range but at its LOWER edge; nothing I found supports the upper end (10^17 ~= 100 quadrillion/yr ~= 8 quadrillion/month) for 2025 - that would require ~6x current aggregate estimates. The "growing rapidly" clause is strongly supported: Google alone went from 9.7T/month (Apr 2024) to 1.3 quadrillion/month (Oct 2025), ~130x in ~18 months; OpenAI cites 20x in two years; Microsoft 5x YoY. WHERE SOURCES DISAGREE / CAVEATS: (1) Scope ambiguity - Google's figure spans all surfaces (Search/AI Overviews, Gemini app, Vertex API) and is not broken down; The Decoder and Tomasz Tunguz argue it is partly "window dressing" because reasoning models (e.g., Gemini 2.5 Flash) emit ~17x more internal tokens per request, so token counts overstate genuine user activity. (2) "Throughput/processed" mostly means input+output+reasoning+multimodal tokens, NOT just generated output text - if the claim meant only generated output tokens, the figure would be several-fold lower. (3) OpenAI/Anthropic/Chinese-provider numbers are partly estimated ("from thin air" per Tunguz), and OpenRouter's headline "100T" is cumulative ~2-year PLATFORM data, not a global annual figure - easy to misread. (4) No official, audited global total exists; all aggregates are estimates with ~2-3x uncertainty. Net: the claim's order-of-magnitude and direction are correct and defensible, but it is slightly generous on the high side - a tighter statement would be "~10^16 tokens/year in 2025, approaching ~2x10^16 by year-end."

claim: Primary aluminum smelting embodies roughly 13-16 kWh of electricity per kg, and stranded hydropower has historically been monetized by siting smelters at the resource (Iceland, Norway).
bestEstimate: Smelting (Hall-Héroult electrolysis + smelter auxiliaries, AC basis): ~13-15.5 kWh/kg for most modern smelters; global average ~14.0-14.2 kWh/kg (IAI 2018-2021). Best/newest cells ~12.5-13 kWh/kg; worst legacy smelters up to ~17-20 kWh/kg. Thermodynamic minimum ~6.2 kWh/kg. Iceland/Norway siting of smelters at hydropower: confirmed historical fact.
reasoning: I checked both halves independently. (1) Energy intensity: Multiple sources converge on the claim's range. Wikipedia's Hall-Héroult entry gives a theoretical minimum of 6.23 kWh/kg and a typical industrial figure of 15.37 kWh/kg. The International Aluminium Institute (the authoritative industry statistician) reports a global average AC smelting power consumption of ~14,100 kWh/tonne (=14.1 kWh/kg) for recent years (Statista cites ~14,114 kWh/t for 2021; another source gives 14.2 kWh/kg world average for 2018). Industry/engineering sources state best smelters ~13 kWh/kg, world average ~15 kWh/kg, newest cells ~12.5 kWh/kg, and least-efficient up to ~20 kWh/kg. So the claim's '13-16 kWh/kg' is an accurate central band for modern primary smelting, though it slightly understates the worst legacy plants and is marginally above the very best. Two important scope caveats where a careless reader could be misled: (a) this is the electrolysis + auxiliaries (AC smelter gate) figure, NOT cradle-to-gate energy — adding alumina (Bayer) refining and anode/carbon production roughly doubles or more the total primary energy, so '13-16 kWh/kg' is correct ONLY for the smelting step, which the claim does correctly say; (b) AC vs DC basis differ by a few percent (DC excludes rectification/auxiliary losses). Sources broadly agree; the main 'disagreement' is just where one draws the efficiency distribution tails. (2) Stranded/remote hydropower monetized via co-located smelters: well documented. Norway's electrometallurgical industry, including aluminium, was built around 1900-1905 (Norsk Hydro era) on remote hydropower; Iceland followed in the 1920s-30s and built aluminium smelters explicitly to monetize otherwise-unexportable hydro/geothermal energy (ISAL/Straumsvík 1969 by Alusuisse; Alcoa Fjarðaál 2008 powered by the dedicated 690 MW Kárahnjúkar station). Iceland today devotes ~70%+ of its electricity to power-intensive industry, dominated by aluminium, each major smelter paired with hydropower. The 'monetize stranded energy by siting the load at the resource' framing is exactly the historical pattern, and is the same logic later invoked for bitcoin mining in Iceland.
